section.title: Moses Returns to Egypt
section.sectionRationale: The seam runs from Moses' departure from Jethro through the strange night attack at the lodging place to the elders' worship in verse 31, closing the call narrative that began at the bush before the first confrontation with Pharaoh in chapter 5.
section.thesis: Even as God commissions Moses to demand Pharaoh release His firstborn son Israel, God nearly takes Moses' own life for neglecting the covenant sign of circumcision, showing that the deliverer himself must first come under the covenant he is sent to enforce.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: Moses' departure and God's warning about Pharaoh's hardened heart; the strange night encounter and Zipporah's circumcision; Aaron's meeting with Moses; the elders believing and worshiping.

verses.text: Then Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said to him, “Please let me return to my brothers in Egypt to see if they are still alive.” “Go in peace,” Jethro replied.
Now the LORD had said to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt, for all the men who sought to kill you are dead.”
So Moses took his wife and sons, put them on a donkey, and headed back to Egypt. And he took the staff of God in his hand.

The LORD instructed Moses, “When you go back to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have put within your power. But I will {{chazaq|harden}} his heart so that he will not let the people go.
Then tell Pharaoh that this is what the LORD says: ‘Israel is My {{bekor|firstborn son}},
and I told you to let My son go so that he may worship Me. But since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son!’”

units.label: The bridegroom of blood
units.note: the deliverer under the covenant sign

verses.text: Now at a lodging place along the way, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him.
But Zipporah took a flint knife, cut off her son's foreskin, and touched it to Moses' feet. “Surely you are a {{chatan-damim|bridegroom of blood}} to me,” she said.
So the LORD let him alone. (When she said, “bridegroom of blood,” she was referring to the circumcision.)

units.label: Reunion and belief
units.note: Aaron meets Moses; the elders worship

verses.text: Meanwhile, the LORD had said to Aaron, “Go and meet Moses in the wilderness.” So he went and met Moses at the mountain of God and kissed him.
And Moses told Aaron everything the LORD had sent him to say, and all the signs He had commanded him to perform.
Then Moses and Aaron went and assembled all the elders of the Israelites,
and Aaron relayed everything the LORD had said to Moses. And Moses performed the signs before the people,
and they believed. And when they heard that the LORD had attended to the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed down and worshiped.

chazaq.gloss: To strengthen or make firm, here rendered harden. This is the first of the hardening statements about Pharaoh's heart in Exodus, and it is God's own declared intention before Moses ever arrives in Egypt.

bekor.gloss: Firstborn. Israel is God's firstborn son by adoption and covenant love, not by natural birth order among the nations, carrying rights of inheritance and a father's special claim, here set against Pharaoh's own coming firstborn.

chatan-damim.gloss: Bridegroom of blood. Zipporah's cryptic phrase marks Moses as bound to her, and to the covenant, through the blood of circumcision performed just in time to turn aside the LORD's threat against him.

basic.context: Moses leaves Midian with his family to return to Egypt as God commanded. On the way, in a strange and unsettling scene, the LORD moves to kill Moses, and Moses' wife Zipporah saves him by circumcising their son. Moses then reunites with his brother Aaron, and together they persuade the elders of Israel that God has heard their cry.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history, including one of its strangest and most debated scenes, the LORD's threat against Moses. It teaches that God takes the covenant sign of circumcision with total seriousness, even for the man He has just commissioned to lead His people.
basic.originalLanguages: God calls Israel His bekor, firstborn son, setting up the coming plague on Pharaoh's own firstborn. And God says He will chazaq, harden or strengthen, Pharaoh's heart, language that will recur again and again through the plague narrative. Zipporah's strange phrase, chatan damim, bridegroom of blood, marks Moses as bound to the covenant by blood just in time.
basic.typology: Israel as God's firstborn son anticipates Christ, the true and greater firstborn, Colossians 1:15, 18, through whom all who believe are adopted as God's children. The threat of death averted by blood at the door of the lodging place anticipates the blood on the doorposts at Passover just chapters later.
basic.christ: God calling Israel His firstborn son points forward to Jesus, the firstborn over all creation, who alone perfectly fulfills sonship, and through whom believers are adopted as sons and daughters, Romans 8:15-17. The blood that turns aside death here previews the Passover blood, itself fulfilled in the blood of Christ.
basic.god: God is both fiercely committed to His covenant people, calling them His own son, and utterly serious about covenant obedience, even from His own chosen deliverer. He is a Father who disciplines those He loves and who provides a way of escape from judgment through blood.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 17:9-14 established circumcision as the covenant sign Abraham's household could not neglect. Exodus 12:13 later has blood on the doorposts turning aside the destroyer. Romans 8:29 calls Christ the firstborn among many brothers.
basic.oneStory: This is a sobering reminder woven into the exodus story: God's deliverer must himself submit to the covenant before he can lead others into it. It anticipates the ultimate pattern of the whole Bible, that only blood turns aside deserved judgment, fulfilled finally in the blood of Christ.

context.literary:
Exodus 4:18-31 is a journey in three stages, and each stage turns on a meeting. Moses meets Jethro and asks leave to go, verse 18. The LORD meets Moses at the lodging place and seeks to kill him, verse 24. Aaron meets Moses at the mountain of God and kisses him, verse 27. The same Hebrew verb stands behind 'met' in verses 24 and 27, so the passage sets two meetings on the road side by side: one that threatens, one that embraces.

The first stage ends with a speech that looks far ahead. Before Moses has even arrived in Egypt, God tells him the end of the story: Pharaoh's heart will be hardened, and because Pharaoh refuses to release God's firstborn son, God will kill Pharaoh's firstborn, verses 21 to 23. The last plague, Exodus 11 and 12, is announced before the first. The reader enters the contest knowing where it will finish.

That speech is immediately followed by the strange night scene of verses 24 to 26, and the placement is deliberate. The word 'firstborn son' in verses 22 and 23 is followed at once by Moses' own son, and a threat of death is followed by blood that turns it aside. The scene is told in three verses with almost no explanation, and the pronouns are left ambiguous, 'him' and 'his feet,' as the BSB footnotes point out. The narrator adds only one note, verse 26, explaining the phrase 'bridegroom of blood.'

The third stage resolves the objections of 3:1-4:17. Moses had feared the people would not believe him, 4:1, and had pleaded that he could not speak, 4:10. Now Aaron speaks, Moses performs the signs, and 'they believed,' verse 31. The chapter ends in worship, the first time Israel bows down in the book. It is a high point that the next chapter will immediately test.
context.historical:
Moses asks Jethro's permission to go, verse 18, because he lived in his father-in-law's household and owed him respect as head of the clan; he does not mention the burning bush, only a wish to see his brothers. Jethro's 'Go in peace' releases him with blessing. The note in verse 19 that 'all the men who sought to kill you are dead' reaches back to Exodus 2:15 and 2:23. The king who wanted Moses dead has died, and a new king sits on the throne.

The family travels on a donkey, verse 20, a modest way to return to a land Moses had left as a prince. The 'lodging place' of verse 24 is the word used for the place where Joseph's brothers stopped on the road, Genesis 42:27: a campsite or wayside stopping place rather than an inn.

Circumcision was practised by several peoples of the ancient Near East, Egypt among them, as Jeremiah 9:25-26 reflects. For Israel it had a unique meaning as the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, commanded on the eighth day, Genesis 17:10-12, and the uncircumcised male 'will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant,' Genesis 17:14. Zipporah uses a flint knife, as Joshua later did at Gilgal, Joshua 5:2-3. Flint remained the traditional tool for the rite long after metal blades were common. That a Midianite woman performs it, and seems to know what is needed, suggests the problem was understood in the household. Exodus 18:2 later says Moses had sent Zipporah back to Jethro, which may mean she returned to Midian after this episode.

The claim 'Israel is My firstborn son' had sharp edges in Egypt. The firstborn was the heir, entitled to a double portion, Deuteronomy 21:17. Pharaoh's royal titles presented him as a son of the sun god, and his own firstborn was heir to the throne. God's message sets His son against Pharaoh's son. Exodus 11:5 names the stakes exactly: 'from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill.'
context.canonical:
The claim of verse 22 runs through the whole Old Testament. God orders every firstborn in Israel to be consecrated to Him because He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, Exodus 13:2 and 13:15, and He takes the Levites in their place, Numbers 3:12-13. Jeremiah 31:9 recalls the relationship in exile: 'I am Israel's Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn.' Hosea 11:1 looks back to this very moment: 'When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.'

The night attack has companions in Genesis and Numbers. Jacob, returning to the land after years away, is met at night by a man who wrestles with him, Genesis 32:24-30. Balaam, riding his donkey on a journey God has permitted, is opposed on the road by the angel of the LORD, Numbers 22:22. In each case a man on his way to fulfil a role in God's purposes is confronted by God Himself before he arrives.

The circumcision theme also develops. Joshua 5:2-9 records a mass circumcision before Israel enters the land, and the Passover law forbids any uncircumcised man to eat, Exodus 12:48. Moses later calls Israel to 'circumcise your hearts,' Deuteronomy 10:16, and promises that the LORD will do it Himself, Deuteronomy 30:6. Paul takes this up: 'circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit,' Romans 2:29, and believers are circumcised in Christ 'with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11.

The New Testament applies the firstborn language to Jesus. Matthew quotes Hosea 11:1 of the child brought back from Egypt, Matthew 2:15, and echoes Exodus 4:19 when the angel tells Joseph that 'those seeking the Child's life are now dead,' Matthew 2:20. Paul calls Christ 'the firstborn over all creation' and 'firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:15 and 1:18, and Hebrews speaks of the church as 'the congregation of the firstborn,' Hebrews 12:23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants Israel to know three things before the confrontation with Pharaoh begins. First, that the outcome is certain. God tells Moses the last plague before the first one falls, verses 21 to 23, so that no hardening of Pharaoh's heart, however long it lasts, will be read as God losing control. The long contest of chapters 5 to 12 unfolds inside a plan God has already announced.

Second, that Israel's identity is sonship before it is nationhood. 'Israel is My firstborn son' comes before Sinai, before the law, before the land. The exodus is not a contract dispute over labour; it is a Father reclaiming His child from a false master who has kept him in slavery.

Third, that the covenant sign matters for the covenant leader. The strange scene at the lodging place is told so that Israel will never think Moses was above the covenant he mediated. The man who would bring Israel out to serve God had himself to come under the sign God gave Abraham. The first hearers, who practised circumcision as their mark of belonging, would have felt the weight of it: even Moses was not exempt, and the life of the deliverer was spared only by covenant blood.

The closing verses then show that God keeps His word to a doubting servant. What He promised in 3:18 and 4:8, that the elders would listen and believe, happens exactly.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records unique events: a direct command to return to Egypt, a divine hardening announced in advance, and a night attack averted by an emergency circumcision. None of these is a pattern for ordinary life, and Christians are not under the command of circumcision, since in Christ they are circumcised 'by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11.

What carries forward is the principle behind the event. Those who lead God's people must themselves be obedient to God; Moses and Aaron would later be kept from the land for failing to honour God before the people, Numbers 20:12. God disciplines those He loves, Hebrews 12:5-6, and He does not exempt those closest to His work. The scene also shows that obedience at home matters: the failure was in Moses' own household.

Verse 31 gives a model that does carry forward directly. When Israel heard that the LORD had attended to them and seen their affliction, they bowed and worshiped. Hearing of God's care is meant to lead to faith and to worship, before deliverance has yet arrived.

debates.question: Why did the LORD seek to kill Moses at the lodging place?

views.label: Moses' neglect of circumcising his son
views.case: The remedy, Zipporah's circumcision of the son and her explanatory statement, strongly implies Moses had failed to keep this basic covenant sign in his own household. Genesis 17:14 says the uncircumcised male has broken the covenant, and verse 26 connects the reprieve directly with the circumcision.

views.label: A broader failure of obedience or readiness
views.case: Some read the episode as testing whether the one about to demand Pharaoh's obedience to God was himself living in full covenant obedience, of which circumcision was the visible sign. The placement right after God's threat against Pharaoh's firstborn suggests that God's judgment falls on disobedience wherever it is found, including in Moses' tent.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge on the same lesson: God will not use an instrument in open covenant disobedience to confront Pharaoh's disobedience, and the remedy, applying the covenant sign, is what turns aside the threat.

debates.question: Whom did the LORD seek to kill, and whose feet did Zipporah touch?

views.label: Moses
views.case: The BSB supplies 'Moses' where the Hebrew says only 'him,' verse 24. Moses is the subject of the surrounding narrative, verses 18 to 23 and 27, and the danger to the leader best explains the urgency. On this view Zipporah touches the foreskin to Moses' body, applying the blood of the covenant to him on his son's behalf.

views.label: Moses' son
views.case: The immediately preceding verse speaks of God killing Pharaoh's firstborn son, verse 23, and the one who was uncircumcised was the boy. Some read 'him' as the son, so that the scene previews the Passover threat against the firstborn and its aversion by blood.

debates.bearing: The BSB follows the majority view that Moses was the one under threat, and the footnotes honestly flag that the Hebrew says 'him' and 'his feet.' Either way, the scene ties together firstborn, blood and deliverance just before the Passover, and shows that God's people are spared by blood applied at His command.

debates.question: If God hardens Pharaoh's heart, verse 21, is Pharaoh still responsible?

views.label: God confirms what Pharaoh chooses
views.case: In the narrative that follows, Pharaoh hardens his own heart several times, Exodus 8:15 and 8:32, and God's hardening comes later, Exodus 9:12. On this view God gives Pharaoh over to the stubbornness he has already chosen, as a judgment.

views.label: God's sovereign purpose
views.case: God announces the hardening before Moses reaches Egypt, verse 21 and Exodus 7:3, and Paul reads it as God's freedom: 'He hardens whom He wants to harden,' Romans 9:17-18. God raised Pharaoh up to display His power and make His name known.

debates.bearing: Exodus holds both without resolving the tension: God is sovereign over Pharaoh's heart, and Pharaoh is fully guilty for his refusal. The two are not competitors. The text never lets Pharaoh plead that God made him do it, and never lets the reader think Pharaoh's stubbornness surprised God.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 24 says the LORD 'was about to kill him.' The Hebrew is literally 'sought to kill him,' using baqash, to seek. It is the verb of Exodus 2:15, 'he sought to kill Moses,' and of verse 19, 'all the men who sought to kill you are dead.' The irony is deliberate. Moses is told that the men who sought his life are dead, and at the very next stopping place the LORD Himself seeks it. The danger Moses must reckon with is no longer Pharaoh; it is God.

The verb 'met,' pagash, appears in verse 24, 'the LORD met Moses,' and again in verse 27, where Aaron 'met Moses at the mountain of God.' The narrator uses the same form for both meetings. The two encounters on the road frame the covenant sign: the one who comes under it is met by God in threat and then by his brother in welcome.

The phrase 'bridegroom of blood,' chatan damim, verse 25, is the passage's great puzzle. The word chatan, bridegroom, shares its root with choten, father-in-law, the word used for Jethro in verse 18, 'his father-in-law.' The root has to do with relation by marriage. Zipporah's words seem to mean that through the blood of the rite her husband is given back to her, bound to her anew by covenant blood. The narrator's note in verse 26 ties the phrase to circumcision, and the plural damim, 'bloods,' is the usual form for shed blood.

Verse 26 says the LORD 'let him alone.' The verb is raphah, to slacken or let go, the verb Pharaoh will use in the next chapter when he calls Israel 'lazy' and 'slackers,' Exodus 5:8 and 5:17. God's letting go of Moses is mercy; Pharaoh's charge of slackness is contempt.

In verse 21 God says He will 'harden' Pharaoh's heart, and the BSB footnote gives the range: 'stiffen or strengthen.' The verb is chazaq, to make strong or firm. The narrative that follows uses two other verbs as well. In Exodus 7:3 God says He will harden Pharaoh's heart with qashah, to make hard or stubborn, the root of the later phrase 'stiff-necked.' In Exodus 8:15 Pharaoh 'hardened his heart' with kaved, to make heavy, the same word used of Moses' 'heavy' mouth in 4:10 and of God's glory. The three verbs together describe a heart made firm, hard and heavy against God.

Finally, verse 23: 'Let My son go so that he may worship Me.' The verb is abad, to serve. Israel is serving Pharaoh as slaves; God demands that His son be released to serve Him. The same verb covers the labour of the brick kilns and the worship of the sanctuary. The question of the exodus is not whether Israel will serve, but whom. And in verse 31 the response to God's care is two verbs together, 'bowed down and worshiped,' qadad and shachah, the pair that recurs when Israel hears the Passover explained, Exodus 12:27.

typology.fulfillment: Israel is called God's son and brought out of Egypt, Hosea 11:1. Matthew applies the verse to Jesus returning from Egypt, Matthew 2:15, presenting Him as the true Israel who relives the nation's story and succeeds where it failed. He is 'the firstborn over all creation' and 'firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:15 and 1:18. The escalation is that Israel was a son by adoption and often disobedient, while Jesus is the eternal Son who always does what pleases the Father. Through Him believers receive 'our adoption as sons,' Galatians 4:5, and become 'the congregation of the firstborn,' Hebrews 12:23.

typology.type: Blood that turns away the destroyer, Exodus 4:25-26
typology.fulfillment: At the lodging place the LORD seeks a life, and blood applied at His command turns Him away. A few chapters later the same shape appears on a national scale: 'when I see the blood, I will pass over you,' Exodus 12:13. The pattern culminates in Christ, whose blood is the blood of the new covenant, Luke 22:20, and who has 'released us from our sins by His blood,' Revelation 1:5. The type falls short because the blood of circumcision was the son's, shed for the father's sake, whereas in the gospel the Father gives His own Son, and the Son's blood is shed for the sons.

typology.type: The firstborn of Egypt taken in exchange for God's firstborn, Exodus 4:23
typology.fulfillment: God warns that because Pharaoh will not release His son, He will take Pharaoh's son. The logic is one firstborn for another. The gospel reverses it. To release His people from slavery, God does not take the firstborn of His enemies; He gives His own. 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The death that fell on Egypt's firstborn as judgment fell on God's firstborn as sacrifice, so that the enemies of God might become His children, John 1:12.

typology.type: The bridegroom bound by blood, Exodus 4:25
typology.fulfillment: Zipporah calls Moses a bridegroom of blood, a husband given back to her through covenant blood. The New Testament calls Jesus the bridegroom, Mark 2:19-20, and says He loved the church and 'gave Himself up for her,' Ephesians 5:25, purchasing her 'with His own blood,' Acts 20:28. The New Testament never cites this verse, so the link is an echo of language rather than a declared type. The contrast is instructive: at the lodging place another's blood saved the bridegroom; at the cross the Bridegroom's own blood saves His bride.

study.christ:
Matthew tells the childhood of Jesus with this passage in mind. When Herod dies, the angel tells Joseph, 'Get up! Take the Child and His mother and go to the land of Israel, for those seeking the Child's life are now dead,' Matthew 2:20. The words recall Exodus 4:19-20, where the LORD tells Moses that 'all the men who sought to kill you are dead,' and Moses takes his wife and sons and sets out. Matthew has just quoted Hosea 11:1, 'Out of Egypt I called My Son,' Matthew 2:15, and Hosea 11:1 itself echoes Exodus 4:22. Jesus is presented as both the new Moses who returns to deliver and the true Son whom God calls out of Egypt.

The passage leads to Christ most clearly through sonship. God's claim on Israel as firstborn is the ground of the whole exodus. But Israel, the son, repeatedly failed. Jesus is the Son in whom the Father is well pleased, the 'firstborn over all creation,' Colossians 1:15, 'the firstborn from the dead,' Revelation 1:5. Through Him sonship is given to others: 'God sent His Son... to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons,' Galatians 4:4-5.

It leads to Christ by contrast in the matter of the firstborn's death. In Exodus God threatens Pharaoh's firstborn to free His own. At the cross the Father gives up His own Son to free His enemies. Romans 8:32 draws the contrast without naming Exodus: 'He who did not spare His own Son.' Isaiah 53:10 says 'it was the LORD's will to crush Him.' The judgment that Egypt's firstborn suffered was borne willingly by God's.

It also leads to Christ through circumcision and blood. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day, Luke 2:21, entering the covenant of Abraham under the law, Galatians 4:4. He fulfilled the sign that Moses had neglected. Then by His death He brought a circumcision 'not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11, the cutting away of the sinful nature. His blood is 'the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20, recalling the covenant blood Moses would sprinkle at Sinai, Exodus 24:8.

Finally, the reunion and belief of verses 27 to 31 anticipate the gospel's own movement. Aaron speaks, the signs are done, and the people believe and worship because they hear that the LORD has seen their affliction. John writes his Gospel so that readers may believe through the signs, John 20:31.

Some Christian readers have made the night attack an elaborate allegory of the cross. The text does not support that. The honest link is the pattern: God's judgment against covenant breaking is real, and blood applied by His command turns it aside.
study.god:
This passage shows God as a Father who claims His child. 'Israel is My firstborn son' is not the language of an employer or a distant deity; it is family language. God's zeal against Pharaoh is the zeal of a father whose son is held in slavery. His demand is personal: 'Let My son go.' The same love appears later in Hosea 11:1 and Jeremiah 31:9. The doctrine of God's fatherhood does not begin in the New Testament; it begins here.

God is also sovereign over the outcome of history. He tells Moses exactly how the confrontation will go before it starts: the wonders, the hardening, the refusal, the death of the firstborn, verses 21 to 23. The story that follows will be long and full of reversals, but nothing in it will surprise God. Paul draws from this that God raised Pharaoh up 'that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth,' Romans 9:17. God's purpose in the exodus is not only Israel's freedom but His own glory among the nations.

God is holy and takes His covenant seriously. The night scene is disturbing precisely because it shows that closeness to God's purposes does not exempt anyone from God's holiness. Moses had heard God's voice at the bush and received His name, yet he was not beyond God's judgment. The LORD who seeks Moses' life is the same LORD who promised 'I will be with you.' His presence is life to the obedient and danger to the careless.

The passage holds judgment and mercy together. God seeks to kill, and then He 'let him alone,' verse 26. The judgment is real, and the way of escape is also His. He does not leave Moses to die; He provides the means by which the threat is lifted, as He will at Passover with the blood on the doorframes, Exodus 12:13 and 12:23.

God keeps His word to the doubting. Moses had objected that the people would not believe, 4:1, and God had promised signs and Aaron. At the close of the chapter every provision is in place: Aaron comes, the signs are done, the people believe. God answers weak faith not with a lecture but with faithfulness.

For worship, the passage teaches Israel's response in verse 31: to bow down when we hear that God has attended to us and seen our affliction. The ground of worship is not first what God has already done but the news that He has seen and will act. Believers worship the Father who calls them His children, and they come under His covenant with reverence.

crossReferences.note: The covenant of circumcision given to Abraham: every male circumcised on the eighth day, and the uncircumcised male cut off, for he has broken the covenant. This is the law Moses' household had failed to keep, and it explains why the threat at the lodging place is lifted only when the sign is applied.

Jacob, returning to the land after years away, is met at night by a man who wrestles with him and leaves him limping but blessed. Like Moses, Jacob is confronted by God on the journey home, before he can face his brother. Both scenes show God dealing with His servant before the servant deals with others.

God will strike every firstborn in Egypt and execute judgment on its gods, but 'when I see the blood, I will pass over you.' The threat announced in Exodus 4:23 is carried out, and the pattern of the lodging place, death turned aside by blood, becomes the pattern of the whole nation's salvation.

Israel's firstborn are consecrated and redeemed because the LORD killed Egypt's firstborn when Pharaoh refused to let Israel go. The father is to explain it to his son. The sonship claimed in Exodus 4:22 becomes a lasting rite in Israel's homes.

'When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.' Hosea recalls the claim of Exodus 4:22 to show God's tender love for an ungrateful people. The verse becomes the bridge by which Matthew applies Israel's sonship to Jesus.

After Herod's death the angel tells Joseph that 'those seeking the Child's life are now dead,' and Joseph takes the Child and His mother back to Israel. The wording echoes Exodus 4:19-20 closely, presenting Jesus as one whose early life retraces Moses' return to deliver his people.

Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh, 'I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you,' and concludes that God hardens whom He wants to harden. He reads the hardening announced in Exodus 4:21 as an expression of God's freedom and His purpose to make His name known.

Believers are circumcised in Christ, 'with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands,' through union with Him in His death and resurrection. The sign that saved Moses' life at the lodging place finds its fulfilment in the inward cutting away of the sinful nature.

Moses promises that the LORD will circumcise the hearts of His people and their descendants so that they love Him and live. The outward sign Zipporah applied in haste is shown to point beyond itself to a work only God can do in the heart.

Christ is 'the firstborn over all creation' and 'firstborn from among the dead.' The title given to Israel in Exodus 4:22 is given to the Son in its fullest sense, marking His supremacy and His resurrection, so that in all things He may have preeminence.

'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' In Exodus God takes the firstborn of His enemy to free His own son. In the gospel He gives His own Son to free His enemies. The contrast shows how far the gospel goes beyond the exodus.

At the sea Israel 'feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.' The belief of Exodus 4:31, based on signs and a report, deepens after the deliverance itself. The two verses frame the exodus: faith at the start, stronger faith at the end.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning the Bible describes the relationship between God and humanity in family terms. Adam is called 'the son of God,' Luke 3:38, and the fall broke that sonship as well as the garden. In Genesis God began to rebuild a family through Abraham, promising that his seed would bless the nations. This passage names the result: Israel, the family of Abraham, is God's firstborn son. The exodus is the story of God rescuing His son.

The passage looks back to Abraham in another way. The covenant sign given in Genesis 17 is not a formality. The one who will lead the family out of Egypt must bear it in his own household, or be cut off. Covenant belonging is marked by blood, and the threat of death is lifted by blood. That pattern, set here in a single tent, will be written on every Israelite door at Passover and in every sacrifice at the tabernacle.

It also looks ahead. The firstborn of Egypt will die, and Israel's firstborn will be spared and then consecrated to God. Israel will be called to be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation,' Exodus 19:6, a son who shows the world what the Father is like. But Israel, like Adam, will prove a disobedient son, and the prophets will speak of a Father grieving over a wayward child, Hosea 11:1-2.

The story reaches its centre in Jesus, the true and obedient Son. He is called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15. He is circumcised under the law, Luke 2:21. He is the firstborn who is not spared, Romans 8:32, and whose blood is the blood of the new covenant, Luke 22:20. Through Him the sonship that Adam lost and Israel failed to live out is given to all who believe, John 1:12, with the Spirit crying 'Abba, Father!' in their hearts, Galatians 4:6.

The story ends in the new creation, where the whole family of God is gathered. The creation itself waits for 'the revelation of the sons of God,' Romans 8:19, and the one who overcomes will hear God say, 'I will be his God, and he will be My son,' Revelation 21:7. The firstborn son of Exodus 4:22 becomes a countless family, and the Father who fought for His child brings every one of them home.

quiz.q: What did God tell Moses to say to Pharaoh regarding Israel?

options.text: Israel belongs to Pharaoh and must remain enslaved.
options.note: This is the opposite of God's message; He claims Israel as His own son, not Pharaoh's possession.

options.text: Pharaoh should adopt Israel as his own people.
options.note: The message is a demand for release, not an offer of adoption to Pharaoh.

options.text: No message was given for Pharaoh at this point.
options.note: A specific message is explicitly given in verses 22 to 23.

options.text: Israel is My firstborn son, and Pharaoh must let him go to worship Me.
options.note: Verses 22 to 23 give this exact message, framing the whole conflict as a father's demand for his son's release.

quiz.q: What alarming event happened at the lodging place on the way to Egypt?

options.text: Moses fell seriously ill from travel.
options.note: The text does not describe illness; it describes a direct threat from the LORD.

options.text: Pharaoh's soldiers ambushed Moses' family.
options.note: The threat in this passage comes from the LORD, not from Egyptian soldiers.

options.text: The LORD met Moses and was about to kill him, until Zipporah circumcised their son.
options.note: Verses 24 to 26 record this startling episode and its resolution.

options.text: Nothing unusual happened at the lodging place.
options.note: This is one of the most unusual and debated episodes in the whole book.

quiz.q: What action resolved the threat against Moses' life?

options.text: Moses offered a sacrifice on an altar.
options.note: No altar or sacrifice is mentioned; the resolution comes through circumcision and Zipporah's action.

options.text: Aaron arrived and prayed for Moses.
options.note: Aaron's meeting with Moses happens afterward, at the mountain of God, not at the lodging place.

options.text: Zipporah circumcised their son and touched the foreskin to Moses, invoking the covenant sign.
options.note: Verse 25 records this exact action, after which the LORD let Moses alone.

options.text: Nothing resolved the situation; Moses died.
options.note: The text is explicit that the LORD let Moses alone after the circumcision.

quiz.q: How did the elders of Israel respond when Moses and Aaron spoke to them?

options.text: They had no reaction at all.
options.note: Their belief and worship are explicitly recorded.

options.text: They rejected Moses and Aaron outright.
options.note: The text records belief and worship, not rejection, at this point in the story.

options.text: They believed, and when they heard the LORD had seen their affliction, they bowed down and worshiped.
options.note: Verse 31 records this response directly, following Aaron's message and Moses' signs.

options.text: They demanded more proof before believing anything.
options.note: The signs performed were sufficient; the text says simply that they believed.

quiz.q: What does the firstborn son language in this passage anticipate later in Exodus?

options.text: The building of the tabernacle.
options.note: The tabernacle instructions come much later and are not connected to this firstborn threat.

options.text: Nothing later in Exodus connects to this language.
options.note: The firstborn theme directly anticipates the tenth plague.

options.text: The tenth plague, in which Egypt's firstborn sons die because Pharaoh refused to release God's firstborn, Israel.
options.note: This exact threat, I will kill your firstborn son, verse 23, is fulfilled in the Passover judgment of chapters 11 to 12.

options.text: The giving of the Ten Commandments.
options.note: The Ten Commandments are a later, separate event at Sinai, not directly tied to the firstborn language here.

questions: God calls Israel His firstborn son, claiming them with a father's love and authority. How does knowing you are adopted as God's child through Christ change how you face situations where you feel powerless?

The strange episode at the lodging place shows God takes covenant obedience seriously, even from Moses himself. Is there an area of obedience you have been neglecting that God may be calling you to address before using you further?

Zipporah acted quickly and decisively to save her husband through the covenant sign and blood. Where do you need to act with similar urgency in applying God's provision to a situation of danger or delay?
The elders believed and worshiped once they heard the LORD had seen their affliction. What has God already done in your life that should move you to worship, even before the deliverance is complete?

God's warning about hardening Pharaoh's heart comes before any confrontation even begins. How does knowing God's sovereignty covers even the hardest, most resistant hearts give you hope for someone you are praying will turn to Him?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew verb translated harden, chazaq, can also mean stiffen or strengthen, and it appears alongside a second Hebrew word, kabed, to make heavy, across the plague narrative, giving a fuller picture of the hardening than any single English word captures.

The Hebrew simply says the LORD met him, literally him, leaving some ambiguity about whether Moses or his son is the immediate object of the threat, though the following circumcision of the son and the address to Moses as bridegroom of blood point to Moses as the one in danger.

The Hebrew literally reads touched it to his feet, feet occasionally serving as a euphemism elsewhere in Scripture, though here it most likely refers literally to Moses' feet as the place where Zipporah touched the severed foreskin.
